summary: Labelle Lake Peak once held the Lumsden fire tower; a May 2016 visit report found only its footings and rusted ski-lift remains.

facts.status_note: A May 2016 visit report found only the tower's deteriorated footings and the rusted ski-lift remains on the summit.

access.note: The visit report describes a walk from Nelson Lake Road on a rough ATV trail. It says nothing about gates, closure or ownership.

visit.trail_note: Park where Nelson Lake Road turns rough; the ATV trail reaches the summit about 1.1 km from the road.

events.note: Visit report posted May 2016: the ski-lift remains were rusted and the tower's footings deteriorated.

evidence.supports: Labelle Lake Peak once had a ski hill and the Lumsden fire tower
evidence.quote: Labelle Lake Peak was once home to both a ski hill and the Lumsden fire tower.

evidence.supports: Peak's listed height is 487 m (1,598 ft)
2016 visit: only rusted ski-lift remains and deteriorated tower footings are left
evidence.quote: Today, the only reminders of these structures are the rusted remains of the ski lifts and the deteriorated footings of the fire tower.

evidence.supports: Summit views south over the Sudbury Basin
evidence.quote: views (south) of the Sudbury Basin can be found

evidence.supports: Park where the road turns rough; only high-clearance vehicles should go further
evidence.quote: The road beyond is in rough condition and it is recommended to park here as only high clearance vehicles should attempt to go further.

evidence.supports: Rough ATV trail climbs almost 400 ft to the summit
evidence.quote: Follow the rough ATV trail as it passes under a hydro-electric power line and ascends almost 400 feet to the summit.

evidence.supports: Summit about 1.1 km from Nelson Lake Road
evidence.quote: About 1.1 km from Nelson Lake Road, the trail reaches the summit

evidence.supports: The 2018 comment says the road is much better to reach
evidence.quote: the road is much better getting there

evidence.supports: Most Ontario towers were erected between the 1920s and the 1950s
evidence.quote: Most of the towers were erected between the 1920's and the 1950's when forest fire protection was in it's heyday.

evidence.supports: Towers were under Lands and Forests, which became the MNR in 1972
evidence.quote: They came under the jurisdiction of Ontario's former Department of Lands and Forests which became the Ministry of Natural Resources in 1972.

evidence.supports: Lookouts were used less through the 1960s as aerial spotting and fire-fighting crews took over
evidence.quote: As the 1960's progressed the towers were in use less and less as aerial fire spotting and fire fighting crews took over.

sources.title: Ontario's Fire Tower Lookouts: Preserving Their History

notes_for_editor: Brief coordinates 46.707909, -81.130404 match the trip report's summit (N46 42.478 W81 07.839) to within about 20 m, so the register record and this report appear to describe the same site. The geohub MNRF tower dataset in source_pages is a JavaScript app and could not be read. No build year, tower height or staffing was found in any source. The access level public is inferred from the route description only; ownership is not stated. Only one site-specific source was found, and it dates from 2016 (plus a 2018 reader comment about the road).
